## Remark on the Problem Statement

The phrase "a specific type of tridiagonal matrix" is not explicitly defined in the prompt. I will interpret it in the standard, classical sense in which this question is customarily posed: a **real symmetric tridiagonal matrix that is strictly (row) diagonally dominant with positive diagonal entries**. This is the canonical class for which the "always positive eigenvalues" claim is a celebrated theorem, and it is the natural reading of the problem. I prove the claim for this class and then give the sharp converse (the Sylvester/Sturm characterization) to make the answer complete.

---

## Theorem

Let $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be a symmetric tridiagonal matrix

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}
a_1 & b_1 & & & 0\\
b_1 & a_2 & b_2 & &\\
& b_2 & a_3 & \ddots &\\
& & \ddots & \ddots & b_{n-1}\\
0 & & & b_{n-1} & a_n
\end{pmatrix},
$$

with

1. **symmetry**: $A=A^{\top}$ (so the only off-diagonal entries are $b_1,\dots,b_{n-1}$ on the two adjacent diagonals), and
2. **strict diagonal dominance with positive diagonal**: $a_i>0$ for all $i$, and
   $$
   a_i \;>\; |b_{i-1}|+|b_i|,\qquad i=1,\dots,n,
   $$
   where we set $b_0=b_n:=0$.

Then **every eigenvalue of $A$ is strictly positive**; equivalently, $A$ is symmetric positive definite.

---

## Proof

### Step 1. Eigenvalues are real.

Because $A$ is real symmetric, $A=A^{\top}$. A standard fact from linear algebra states that every eigenvalue of a real symmetric matrix is real, and $A$ admits an orthonormal eigenbasis. Hence we may speak unambiguously of the eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\in\mathbb{R}$.

### Step 2. Gershgorin localizes the spectrum.

Apply the **Gershgorin circle theorem** to the rows of $A$. The $i$-th Gershgorin disc is

$$
D_i \;=\; \bigl\{\,z\in\mathbb{C}\;:\;|z-a_i|\le R_i\,\bigr\},
\qquad
R_i \;:=\; \sum_{j\neq i}|a_{ij}|.
$$

Because $A$ is tridiagonal, the only off-diagonal entries in row $i$ are $a_{i,i-1}=b_{i-1}$ (when $i\ge2$) and $a_{i,i+1}=b_i$ (when $i\le n-1$). Therefore

$$
R_i \;=\; |b_{i-1}|+|b_i|,
\qquad\text{with } b_0=b_n:=0.
$$

By the strict diagonal dominance hypothesis (2),

$$
R_i \;=\; |b_{i-1}|+|b_i| \;<\; a_i \qquad\text{for every }i.
$$

Gershgorin's theorem guarantees

$$
\sigma(A)\;\subseteq\;\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}D_i.
$$

### Step 3. Every Gershgorin disc lies strictly in the open right half-plane.

Each $D_i$ is a closed disc centered at $a_i>0$ with radius $R_i<a_i$. For any $z\in D_i$,

$$
\operatorname{Re}(z)\;\ge\;a_i-|z-a_i|\;\ge\;a_i-R_i\;>\;0.
$$

Thus $D_i\subset\{z:\operatorname{Re}z>0\}$ for every $i$, and consequently

$$
\sigma(A)\;\subset\;\bigcup_i D_i\;\subset\;\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\operatorname{Re}z>0\}.
$$

### Step 4. Combine Steps 1 and 3.

From Step 1, every eigenvalue $\lambda_k$ is real. From Step 3, every eigenvalue satisfies $\operatorname{Re}(\lambda_k)>0$. For a real number, $\operatorname{Re}(\lambda_k)=\lambda_k$, so

$$
\lambda_k \;>\; 0\qquad\text{for all }k=1,\dots,n.
$$

Hence $A$ is symmetric positive definite, and all of its eigenvalues are strictly positive. $\blacksquare$

---

## Sharpness and the Converse (Sturm/Sylvester characterization)

The strict inequality in the diagonal-dominance hypothesis is essential: dropping it breaks the conclusion. For example,

$$
\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}
$$

is symmetric tridiagonal with positive diagonal and *weak* diagonal dominance ($a_i=|b_{i-1}|+|b_i|$), yet its eigenvalues are $2$ and $0$ — not strictly positive. With a larger off-diagonal, e.g.

$$
\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix},
$$

the eigenvalues are $3$ and $-1$, so positivity fails outright. Thus strict diagonal dominance is a genuine sufficient condition, not a necessary one, and the margin $a_i-|b_{i-1}|-|b_i|>0$ is exactly what Gershgorin uses.

For completeness, the **exact** characterization of positive definiteness for a symmetric tridiagonal matrix is given by Sylvester's criterion specialized via a three-term recurrence. Define the leading principal minors $D_0:=1$ and

$$
D_k \;:=\; \det A[1:k,1:k],\qquad k=1,\dots,n.
$$

Expanding along the last column (only two non-zero entries, $a_k$ and $b_{k-1}$, appear) gives the recurrence

$$
D_k \;=\; a_k\,D_{k-1} \;-\; b_{k-1}^{\,2}\,D_{k-2},\qquad k\ge1,\quad D_{-1}:=0,\;D_0:=1.
$$

A symmetric tridiagonal matrix is positive definite **if and only if**

$$
D_k>0\quad\text{for every }k=1,\dots,n.
$$

This is exactly Sylvester's criterion; the recurrence above is the efficient way to evaluate it for tridiagonal structure, and it is the classical **Sturm sequence** recurrence. The Gershgorin-based proof above is the clean, hypothesis-driven way to guarantee $D_k>0$ for all $k$ in one stroke, since strict diagonal dominance with positive diagonal implies positive definiteness directly.

---

## Conclusion

For the standard class — a **real symmetric tridiagonal matrix that is strictly row-diagonally dominant with positive diagonal entries** — the eigenvalues are **always strictly positive**. The proof combines the reality of the spectrum (symmetry) with the Gershgorin circle theorem, which forces every eigenvalue into the open right half-plane; reality then promotes "positive real part" to "strictly positive." The condition is sufficient but not necessary; the exact necessary-and-sufficient condition is the positivity of all leading principal minors, computable via the three-term Sturm recurrence $D_k=a_kD_{k-1}-b_{k-1}^2D_{k-2}$.
